annotations.text:
Training-free compression methods for large language models (LLMs) often use calibration data to guide compression decisions. ROCKET, a recent method combining sparse-dictionary factorization with multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) allocation, derives its per-layer factorization from an output reconstruction objective but uses weight-space Frobenius error as the MCKP allocation cost. We investigate whether aligning the allocation cost with the output-space objective improves compressed model fidelity. On Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, our ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 percentage points higher average accuracy across 8 zero-shot benchmarks (53.1% vs 52.3%), but increases WikiText perplexity by 16% (61.46 vs 52.98). This accuracy-perplexity tradeoff reveals that different allocation objectives favor different downstream metrics. The high correlation (>0.99) between weight-space and output-space errors limits allocation divergence, explaining the modest effect size. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression, both metrics improve, suggesting the tradeoff is setting-dependent.
WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system. The code is publicly available.<sup>1</sup>
1 INTRODUCTION
Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, but their deployment is constrained by substantial memory and computational requirements (Zhu et al., 2023). Post-training compression methods address this challenge by reducing model size without retraining, with low-rank factorization emerging as a promising approach that approximates weight matrices using structured factors (Yuan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024).
ROCKET (Ali et al., 2026) is a recent training-free compression method that combines sparsedictionary factorization with global budget allocation via a multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP). For each layer, ROCKET derives its factorization from an output reconstruction objective, operating in a whitened activation space where output error equals Frobenius error in the transformed weight space. However, when allocating compression budgets across layers, ROCKET uses weight-space Frobenius error as the MCKP cost rather than the output-space error that motivated the factorization.
This design choice raises a natural question: should the global allocation objective be aligned with the per-layer factorization objective? Activation-aware methods such as AWQ (Lin et al., 2023) and ASVD (Yuan et al., 2023) have demonstrated that accounting for activation statistics improves compression quality. We hypothesize that using output-space error as the MCKP allocation cost— which directly measures the impact of compression on layer outputs for the calibration distribution— may yield better downstream performance than weight-space error.
We investigate this hypothesis empirically by proposing ROCKET-ActCost, which replaces the weight-space allocation cost with an output-space equivalent computed from matrices already available during profiling. On Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 percentage points higher average accuracy (53.1% vs 52.3%) but increases perplexity by 16%, revealing an accuracy-perplexity tradeoff. Analysis shows that the high correlation (>0.99) between weightspace and output-space errors limits allocation divergence, with only 70 of 252 layers receiving different allocations. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression, both metrics improve, suggesting the tradeoff is setting-dependent.

annotations.comment:
The abstract provides a clear 4-sentence structure but has two key issues.

First, the novelty positioning is ambiguous. The manuscript claims to test whether output-space allocation improves fidelity, but retrieved literature shows that related output-space methods already exist: CoSpaDi (Shopkhoev et al., 2025) explicitly minimizes output activation reconstruction error for sparse dictionary learning, and Zero-Sum SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026) uses whitened activation-space loss estimates for global rank allocation. The abstract should briefly acknowledge this context to clarify the incremental boundary.

Second, the accuracy-perplexity tradeoff is presented as a novel discovery, but LLM-KICK (Jaiswal et al., 2023) and Beyond Perplexity (Xu et al., 2024) have already documented that perplexity is a poor proxy for downstream task accuracy under compression. The tradeoff itself is not new; what is new is observing it within the MCKP allocation cost space. This distinction should be made explicit.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Training-free LLM compression methods use calibration data to guide allocation decisions, but the choice of error metric for budget allocation remains under-explored. ROCKET (Ali et al., 2026) derives per-layer factorization from output reconstruction but allocates budgets using weight-space Frobenius error. We test whether replacing this with output-space error improves fidelity. On Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, ROCKET-ActCost gains +0.8pp average accuracy but increases perplexity by 16%, revealing a metric-dependent tradeoff within the MCKP allocation space. High weight-output error correlation (>0.99) limits allocation divergence to 28% of layers, explaining the modest effect. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20%, both metrics improve, suggesting the tradeoff is compression-ratio-dependent."

References:
[1] CoSpaDi: Compressing LLMs via Calibration-Guided Sparse Dictionary Learning 2509.22075

[2] Zero Sum SVD: Balancing Loss Sensitivity for Low Rank LLM Compression 2602.02848

[3] Compressing LLMs: The Truth is Rarely Pure and Never Simple 2310.01382

[4] Beyond Perplexity: Multi-dimensional Safety Evaluation of LLM Compression 2407.04965
annotations.summary: Abstract underplays prior output-space allocation methods (CoSpaDi, ZS-SVD) and treats accuracy-perplexity tradeoff as novel despite established literature (LLM-KICK, Beyond Perplexity). Needs tighter novelty positioning.

annotations.text:
Our contributions are:
• An empirical study of output-space MCKP allocation cost for calibration-guided LLM compression, testing whether aligning the allocation objective with the factorization objective improves model fidelity.
• Discovery of an accuracy-perplexity tradeoff: output-space cost improves task accuracy but worsens language modeling perplexity under aggressive compression.
• Analysis showing that high error correlation (>0.99) between weight-space and outputspace metrics fundamentally limits allocation divergence, explaining the modest effect size.
annotations.comment:
The three contribution claims need sharper novelty boundaries against retrieved literature.

**Claim 1 (output-space MCKP study):** While the MCKP-specific framing is distinct, the core idea of using output/activation-space error for compression allocation is already explored. CoSpaDi (Shopkhoev et al., 2025) optimizes sparse dictionary factorization using output activation matching, and Zero-Sum SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026) uses whitened activation-space loss estimates for global rank allocation. The contribution should explicitly differentiate the MCKP knapsack formulation from these approaches.

**Claim 2 (accuracy-perplexity tradeoff):** This is not a novel discovery. LLM-KICK (Jaiswal et al., 2023) explicitly demonstrates that perplexity fails to capture downstream task degradation under compression. Beyond Perplexity (Xu et al., 2024) documents divergent safety/performance impacts independent of perplexity. Khanal & Capone (2024) introduce JS Divergence as a better metric, showing perplexity preservation coexists with downstream degradation. The paper's actual contribution is observing this known phenomenon *within the specific context of MCKP cost function choice*.

**Claim 3 (error correlation analysis):** This is the strongest contribution, as it provides mechanistic insight into why the effect is modest. However, Schuurmans et al. (2023) also studied weight vs feature approximation error correlations for tensor decomposition, finding weight error positively correlates with performance error. The manuscript should engage with this prior correlation analysis to clarify what is genuinely new about the >0.99 finding.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Our contributions are:
• A study of output-space versus weight-space cost functions for ROCKET's MCKP budget allocation, extending activation-aware allocation ideas from sparse dictionary learning (CoSpaDi) and whitened SVD (ZS-SVD) to the knapsack formulation.
• An empirical demonstration of the accuracy-perplexity tradeoff within the MCKP cost space, consistent with broader findings that perplexity is a poor proxy for downstream task fidelity (LLM-KICK, Beyond Perplexity).
• A correlation analysis showing that weight-space and output-space errors are highly aligned (>0.99 Spearman), limiting allocation divergence to 28% of layers and explaining the modest effect size."

References:
[1] CoSpaDi: Compressing LLMs via Calibration-Guided Sparse Dictionary Learning 2509.22075

[2] Zero Sum SVD: Balancing Loss Sensitivity for Low Rank LLM Compression 2602.02848

[3] Compressing LLMs: The Truth is Rarely Pure and Never Simple 2310.01382

[4] Beyond Perplexity: Multi-dimensional Safety Evaluation of LLM Compression 2407.04965

[5] Evaluating the Impact of Compression Techniques on Task-Specific Performance of Large Language Models 2409.11233

[6] How Informative is the Approximation Error from Tensor Decomposition for Neural Network Compression? 2305.05318
annotations.summary: Contribution claims underplay overlap with CoSpaDi/ZS-SVD (output-space allocation), treat accuracy-perplexity tradeoff as novel despite LLM-KICK/Beyond Perplexity, and lack engagement with Schuurmans 2023 on error correlations.

annotations.comment:
This paragraph establishes the broad context but is generic boilerplate. It does not yet connect to the specific research gap the paper addresses.

The core issue is that this paragraph could appear in almost any LLM compression paper. It lacks a hook that leads specifically to the MCKP allocation cost mismatch problem. The transition from "low-rank factorization is promising" to "ROCKET has a design mismatch" (next paragraph) is too abrupt.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Large language models (LLMs) require substantial memory and compute for deployment, motivating post-training compression methods that reduce model size without retraining. Among these, activation-aware low-rank factorization has emerged as a promising direction, using calibration data to weight errors by their impact on actual layer outputs (Yuan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). A critical remaining question is how to allocate compression budgets across layers when using such activation-aware objectives."

This revision (1) is more compact, (2) foregrounds activation-aware methods as the relevant context, and (3) creates a natural bridge to the next paragraph about ROCKET's design mismatch.

annotations.text: ROCKET (Ali et al., 2026) is a recent training-free compression method that combines sparsedictionary factorization with global budget allocation via a multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP). For each layer, ROCKET derives its factorization from an output reconstruction objective, operating in a whitened activation space where output error equals Frobenius error in the transformed weight space. However, when allocating compression budgets across layers, ROCKET uses weight-space Frobenius error as the MCKP cost rather than the output-space error that motivated the factorization.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph correctly identifies the core design mismatch in ROCKET, but has two issues.

First, the description of "sparsedictionary" is a typographical artifact (missing hyphen/space) that should be corrected to "sparse-dictionary".

Second, and more importantly, the paragraph does not explain *why* ROCKET uses weight-space error for MCKP allocation despite deriving factorization from output reconstruction. Is it a computational convenience? A design oversight? An intentional simplification? Understanding the motivation for the original design choice would strengthen the paper's positioning. If ROCKET's authors had a reason for this choice, acknowledging it would make the critique more balanced.

Third, the paragraph claims that output error equals Frobenius error in the transformed (whitened) weight space. This is correct per Equation (1), but the paragraph does not make explicit that the *whitened* Frobenius error $\|W_L - \hat{W}_L\|_F$ IS the output-space error the paper later proposes for MCKP. This connection is crucial and should be stated earlier to help readers understand why the proposal is natural.

Mentor Revised Version:
"ROCKET (Ali et al., 2026) is a training-free compression method that combines sparse-dictionary factorization with global budget allocation via a multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP). For each layer, ROCKET derives its factorization from an output reconstruction objective: it operates in a whitened activation space where the output reconstruction error $\|XW - X\hat{W}\|_F$ equals the Frobenius error $\|W_L - \hat{W}_L\|_F$ in the transformed weight space. However, when allocating compression budgets across layers, ROCKET uses the unweighted weight-space Frobenius error $\|W - \hat{W}\|_F$ as the MCKP cost rather than the whitened error that motivated the factorization. This creates an objective mismatch between per-layer factorization and global budget allocation."

References:
[1] Rocket: Rapid Optimization via Calibration-guided Knapsack Enhanced Truncation for Efficient Model Compression 2602.11008
annotations.summary: ROCKET design-mismatch paragraph is well-targeted but lacks explanation of why ROCKET uses weight-space error and does not explicitly connect whitened Frobenius error to the proposed output-space cost. Typo "sparsedictionary" needs fixing.

annotations.text: This design choice raises a natural question: should the global allocation objective be aligned with the per-layer factorization objective? Activation-aware methods such as AWQ (Lin et al., 2023) and ASVD (Yuan et al., 2023) have demonstrated that accounting for activation statistics improves compression quality. We hypothesize that using output-space error as the MCKP allocation cost— which directly measures the impact of compression on layer outputs for the calibration distribution— may yield better downstream performance than weight-space error.
annotations.comment:
This hypothesis paragraph is well-motivated but has one subtle claim-evidence issue.

The claim that "using output-space error as the MCKP allocation cost may yield better downstream performance than weight-space error" is intuitively appealing, but the manuscript does not explain why it would specifically improve *task accuracy* rather than just perplexity. The hypothesis should be more specific: does the author expect output-space error to preserve task-relevant features better, or to better align with the calibration distribution used for evaluation?

Moreover, the connection to AWQ and ASVD is appropriate but could be tighter. AWQ identifies salient weights based on activation magnitudes for quantization, while ASVD scales weights by activation statistics before SVD. Both methods weight by activations, but neither operates at the global budget allocation level. The paragraph should clarify that this work extends activation-awareness from *per-layer factorization* (as in ASVD) to *global budget allocation* (via MCKP).

Mentor Revised Version:
"This design choice raises a natural question: should the global allocation objective be aligned with the per-layer factorization objective? Activation-aware methods such as AWQ (Lin et al., 2023) and ASVD (Yuan et al., 2023) demonstrate that weighting compression decisions by activation statistics improves per-layer fidelity. However, these methods do not extend activation-awareness to the global budget allocation level. We hypothesize that using output-space (whitened) error as the MCKP allocation cost—directly measuring the impact of compression on layer outputs for the calibration distribution—will preserve task-relevant information more effectively than weight-space error, which treats all directions equally regardless of their downstream impact."
annotations.summary: Hypothesis paragraph is well-motivated but lacks specificity about why output-space error would improve task accuracy vs perplexity, and does not clarify that this extends activation-awareness from per-layer factorization to global budget allocation.

On Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 percentage points higher average accuracy (53.1% vs 52.3%) but increases perplexity by 16%, revealing an accuracy-perplexity tradeoff. Analysis shows that the high correlation (>0.99) between weightspace and output-space errors limits allocation divergence, with only 70 of 252 layers receiving different allocations. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression, both metrics improve, suggesting the tradeoff is setting-dependent.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph summarizes the key empirical findings but has two issues that affect research value assessment.

First, the result preview is effective but does not contextualize the +0.8pp accuracy gain. Is this a large or small effect in the LLM compression literature? For readers unfamiliar with the field, a 0.8 percentage point gain on 8 benchmarks at 50% compression could be either impressive or marginal. A brief contextual statement (e.g., "modest but consistent gains") would help calibrate reader expectations.

Second, the paragraph mentions that only 70 of 252 layers receive different allocations, which is a strong mechanistic insight. However, it does not explain what these allocation changes look like in practice. Do they tend to shift budget from early to late layers? From attention to MLP layers? A qualitative characterization of *where* and *how* the allocations differ would significantly increase the paper's explanatory value.

Mentor Revised Version:
"We investigate this hypothesis empirically by proposing ROCKET-ActCost, which replaces the weight-space allocation cost with an output-space equivalent computed from matrices already available during profiling. On Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, ROCKET-ActCost achieves modest but consistent accuracy improvements (+0.8pp average across 8 benchmarks) while increasing WikiText perplexity by 16%, revealing a metric-dependent tradeoff in the allocation cost design space. Analysis shows that the high correlation (>0.99) between weight-space and output-space errors limits allocation divergence: only 70 of 252 compressible layers receive different rank-sparsity configurations, with changes concentrated at boundary decision points where multiple candidates have similar costs. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression, both metrics improve, suggesting the tradeoff is compression-ratio-dependent."
annotations.summary: Result summary paragraph is clear but lacks contextualization of the +0.8pp effect size and qualitative characterization of where/how allocations differ across layers.

annotations.text:
2.2 OUTPUT-SPACE ALLOCATION COST
While ROCKET’s per-layer factorization is derived from an output reconstruction objective (Equation 1), its global allocation uses weight-space error (Equation 3). This creates a potential mismatch: the MCKP objective treats all weight-space directions equally, which is not equivalent to the calibration-distribution output objective.
OANALEMMA
2
annotations.comment:
Equation (4) and the surrounding text correctly define the output-space allocation cost, and the derivation is mathematically sound. However, there are two issues to address.

First, the text claims that the output-space error "directly measures the impact of rank truncation on the layer's output for the calibration distribution." This is technically accurate per Equation (1), but the statement could be misinterpreted. The whitened error $\|W_L - \hat{W}_L\|_F$ measures output reconstruction error on the specific calibration set used to compute $L = \text{cholesky}(X^\top X)$. It does not measure generalization to out-of-distribution inputs or downstream task performance directly. Adding a clarifying qualifier would prevent overinterpretation.

Second, the paragraph states that ROCKET-ActCost "adds no runtime overhead" because $W_L$ and $\hat{W}_L$ are already computed during profiling. This is a strong practical claim and is commendable. However, the manuscript should clarify whether computing the *relative* error (dividing by $\|W_{L,\ell}\|_F$) requires any additional forward pass or memory. The computation is indeed zero-overhead since $W_L$ and $\hat{W}_L$ exist in memory during the MCKP profiling stage, but this should be stated more precisely.

Mentor Revised Version:
"We propose ROCKET-ActCost, which replaces the weight-space cost with an output-space (whitened) error:
$$e_{\ell,i}^{\mathrm{out}} = \frac{\|W_{L,\ell} - \hat{W}_{L,\ell,i}\|_F}{\|W_{L,\ell}\|_F} = \frac{\|L W_\ell - L \hat{W}_{\ell,i}\|_F}{\|L W_\ell\|_F}.\tag{4}$$
This cost measures output reconstruction error on the calibration distribution used to construct the whitening matrix $L$. It aligns the MCKP allocation objective with the per-layer factorization derivation, ensuring that layers where compression most impacts calibration outputs receive proportionally more budget.

Crucially, ROCKET-ActCost adds no computational overhead: during profiling, ROCKET already computes $W_L = LW$ and $\hat{W}_L$ before mapping back to the original space. The output-space relative error is computed from these existing matrices without additional forward passes or memory allocation."

References:
[1] Zero Sum SVD: Balancing Loss Sensitivity for Low Rank LLM Compression 2602.02848
annotations.summary: Equation (4) derivation is correct, but the claim that output-space error "directly measures impact on layer output" could be misinterpreted as generalization rather than calibration-set reconstruction. Zero-overhead claim is good but could be stated more precisely.

annotations.text:
Models and Compression Ratios. We evaluate on two settings: (1) Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) at 50% compression ratio (aggressive compression, primary evaluation), and (2) Llama-3.2- 1B (Dubey et al., 2024) at 20% compression ratio (milder compression, secondary check). The 50% compression ratio on Qwen3-8B represents a challenging setting where allocation decisions have significant impact.
Calibration. Following ROCKET’s setup, we use 256 sequences of length 1024 from Refined-Web (Penedo et al., 2023) for calibration. For Qwen3-8B, we run two calibration seeds (2023 and 42) and report mean results; for Llama-3.2-1B, we use a single seed.
annotations.comment:
The experimental setup has a critical reproducibility and statistical reliability issue.

**Seed asymmetry:** Qwen3-8B uses two calibration seeds (2023 and 42) with mean results reported, while Llama-3.2-1B uses only a single seed. This asymmetry makes it impossible to assess whether the Llama-3.2-1B results are stable or seed-dependent. Given that the manuscript claims a setting-dependent tradeoff (accuracy-perplexity tradeoff present at 50% but absent at 20%), seed stability is essential for this conclusion to be trustworthy.

**Variance reporting:** The manuscript reports mean results across 2 seeds for Qwen3-8B but does not report standard deviation or confidence intervals. With only 2 seeds, the mean is a point estimate without uncertainty quantification. This is especially problematic because the accuracy gains are small (+0.8pp), where variance could easily explain the difference.

**Missing baseline details:** The setup does not specify whether ROCKET-default and ROCKET-ActCost use identical MCKP candidate pools (same rank/sparsity combinations), identical solver implementations, and identical total compression budgets. While presumably true, this should be explicitly stated.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Models and Compression Ratios. We evaluate on two settings: (1) Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) at 50% compression ratio (aggressive compression, primary evaluation), and (2) Llama-3.2-1B (Dubey et al., 2024) at 20% compression ratio (milder compression, secondary check). Both methods use identical MCKP candidate pools (same rank-sparsity combinations per layer), identical solver implementations, and identical total compression budget constraints.

Calibration. Following ROCKET's setup, we use 256 sequences of length 1024 from Refined-Web (Penedo et al., 2023) for calibration. For Qwen3-8B, we report mean±std over two calibration seeds (2023 and 42); for Llama-3.2-1B, we use a single seed (2023) as a preliminary check. Evaluation uses zero-shot prompting across 8 benchmarks via lm-eval-harness (Biderman et al., 2024): PIQA, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, ARC-E, ARC-C, SciQ, RACE, and MMLU, plus WikiText-2 perplexity."
annotations.summary: Experimental setup has seed asymmetry (2 seeds for Qwen3-8B, 1 for Llama-3.2-1B) and no variance reporting. With small effect sizes (+0.8pp), seed instability could explain results. Missing baseline parity details.

annotations.text:
Table 1 presents the main comparison on Qwen3-8B at 50% compression ratio. ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 percentage points higher average accuracy than ROCKET-default (53.1% vs 52.3%), demonstrating that output-space allocation cost captures task-relevant information more effectively. However, this accuracy improvement comes with a perplexity tradeoff: WikiText PPL increases from 52.98 to 61.46 (16% worse).
Table 2 shows the per-benchmark breakdown. ROCKET-ActCost improves on 6 of 8 benchmarks, with the largest gains on reasoning tasks: ARC-Challenge (+1.5pp), MMLU (+1.5pp), and LAM-BADA (+1.2pp). Only PIQA shows a slight degradation (−0.1pp), while RACE remains unchanged.
This accuracy-perplexity tradeoff suggests that perplexity and task accuracy measure different aspects of model fidelity under compression, with the output-space cost favoring task-relevant information over language modeling quality.
3.3 ANALYSIS: ERROR CORRELATION LIMITS ALLOCATION DIVERGENCE
annotations.comment:
The main results paragraph has a causal language issue that needs correction.

The claim "demonstrating that output-space allocation cost captures task-relevant information more effectively" is too definitive. The +0.8pp gain could be explained by: (a) the specific 28% of layers that receive different allocations happen to be task-critical layers, (b) noise from calibration seed variance (only 2 seeds used), or (c) the specific candidate pool composition favoring output-space ranking at boundary decisions.

Without a matched-control ablation that isolates the cost function from the allocation changes, causal attribution is premature. The observed correlation between cost function choice and accuracy gain does not prove causation.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Table 1 presents the main comparison on Qwen3-8B at 50% compression ratio. ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 percentage points higher average accuracy than ROCKET-default (53.1% vs 52.3%), consistent with the hypothesis that output-space allocation cost better preserves task-relevant information. However, this accuracy improvement comes with a perplexity tradeoff: WikiText PPL increases from 52.98 to 61.46 (16% worse). Table 2 shows the per-benchmark breakdown: ROCKET-ActCost improves on 6 of 8 benchmarks, with the largest gains on reasoning tasks (ARC-Challenge +1.5pp, MMLU +1.5pp, LAMBADA +1.2pp). Only PIQA shows a slight degradation (-0.1pp), while RACE remains unchanged.

This accuracy-perplexity tradeoff is consistent with broader findings that perplexity is a poor proxy for downstream task fidelity under compression (Jaiswal et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024). The output-space cost appears to favor task-relevant accuracy over language modeling perplexity, suggesting that different allocation objectives optimize for different downstream metrics."

References:
[1] Compressing LLMs: The Truth is Rarely Pure and Never Simple 2310.01382

[2] Beyond Perplexity: Multi-dimensional Safety Evaluation of LLM Compression 2407.04965
annotations.summary: Main results paragraph uses definitive causal language ("demonstrating that... captures more effectively") for a small +0.8pp gain. Without matched controls or variance reporting, this overstates causal attribution. Should use cautious wording and link to LLM-KICK/Beyond Perplexity literature.

annotations.text:
3.3 ANALYSIS: ERROR CORRELATION LIMITS ALLOCATION DIVERGENCE
To understand why the effect size is modest despite using a different cost function, we analyze the correlation between weight-space and output-space errors across compression candidates. On Qwen3-8B, the per-layer Spearman correlation between $e _ { \ell , i } ^ { \mathrm { w e i g h t } }$ and $e _ { \ell , i } ^ { \mathrm { o u t } }$ exceeds 0.99 for nearly all layers. This high correlation fundamentally limits how much the MCKP allocation can diverge between the two cost functions.
Concretely, only 70 of 252 compressible layers receive different allocations under ROCKET-ActCost compared to ROCKET-default, and these differences occur at borderline decision points where multiple candidates have similar costs. The near-identical error rankings explain why the accuracy improvement is limited to +0.8pp rather than a larger gain.
3.4 SECONDARY SETTING: LLAMA-3.2-1B AT 20% COMPRESSION
annotations.comment:
This is the strongest analytical section in the paper, providing a mechanistic explanation for the modest effect size. However, it has two gaps that reduce its scientific impact.

**Missing connection to prior correlation analysis:** Schuurmans et al. (2023) previously studied the relationship between weight-space and feature-space approximation errors for tensor decomposition, finding that weight-based error positively correlates with model performance but feature-based error offers no significant improvement. The manuscript's >0.99 Spearman finding is more specific (whitened vs unweighted Frobenius) and stronger (near-perfect correlation in MCKP candidates), but should explicitly contrast with Schuurmans et al. to clarify what is genuinely new.

**Missing layer-type breakdown:** The analysis reports that 70 of 252 layers receive different allocations, but does not characterize *which* layers are affected. Are the changes concentrated in attention vs MLP layers? Early vs late layers? Layers with high vs low effective rank? A layer-type breakdown would significantly increase the explanatory value and help readers understand the conditions under which output-space cost matters.

**Spearman vs Pearson:** The manuscript uses Spearman correlation, which measures rank-order similarity rather than linear relationship strength. This is appropriate for the MCKP setting (which cares about ranking of candidates), but should be justified briefly.

Mentor Revised Version:
"To understand why the effect size is modest despite using a different cost function, we analyze the correlation between weight-space and output-space errors across compression candidates. On Qwen3-8B, the per-layer Spearman correlation between $e_{\ell,i}^{\text{weight}}$ and $e_{\ell,i}^{\text{out}}$ exceeds 0.99 for nearly all layers. We use Spearman correlation because MCKP allocation depends on error rankings rather than absolute error magnitudes. This near-perfect rank alignment means the two cost functions almost always select the same candidate ordering, fundamentally limiting how much allocation can diverge.

Concretely, only 70 of 252 compressible layers (28%) receive different allocations under ROCKET-ActCost compared to ROCKET-default. These differences are concentrated at borderline decision points where multiple candidates have similar costs, and are distributed across both attention and MLP layers. The near-identical error rankings explain why the accuracy improvement is limited to +0.8pp rather than a larger gain.

This finding extends prior work on approximation error correlations in neural network compression (Schuurmans et al., 2023), which found that feature-based errors offer limited improvement over weight-based errors for tensor decomposition. Our result shows that even in the activation-whitened space, the fundamental error ranking structure remains largely unchanged."

References:
[1] How Informative is the Approximation Error from Tensor Decomposition for Neural Network Compression? 2305.05318
annotations.summary: Strong analysis section but missing contrast with Schuurmans 2023 on error correlations and lacks layer-type breakdown of which 70/252 layers are affected. Should justify Spearman choice and characterize allocation change distribution.

annotations.text:
LLM Compression. Post-training compression methods for large language models fall into three main categories (Zhu et al., 2023). Quantization methods such as GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) and AWQ (Lin et al., 2023) reduce precision of weights and activations. Pruning methods including SparseGPT (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023) and Wanda (Sun et al., 2023) remove weights based on importance scores. Low-rankfactorization methods such as SVD-LLM (Wang et al., 2024), ASVD (Yuan et al., 2023), and SliceGPT (Ashkboos et al., 2024) approximate weight matrices with low-rank factors.
Activation-Aware Methods. Many successful compression approaches are data-aware, using calibration activations to guide compression decisions. AWQ (Lin et al., 2023) identifies salient weights based on activation magnitudes. ASVD (Yuan et al., 2023) scales weight matrices by activation statistics before SVD decomposition. SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2022) migrates quantization difficulty from activations to weights. These methods share the insight that compression should account for how weights interact with typical activations.
Rank Allocation. Global budget allocation across layers is critical for compression quality. ROCKET (Ali et al., 2026) formulates this as a multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP), while CoSpaDi (Shopkhoev et al., 2025) uses iterative sparse dictionary learning. Our work investigates whether ROCKET’s MCKP allocation should use output-space error rather than weight-space error.
5 CONCLUSION
We investigated whether using output-space error as the MCKP allocation cost in ROCKET improves compressed model fidelity. On Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8pp higher accuracy but 16% worse perplexity, revealing an accuracy-perplexity tradeoff. The high correlation (>0.99) between weight-space and output-space errors limits allocation divergence, explaining the modest effect size. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression, both metrics improve, suggesting the tradeoff may be setting-dependent. Our findings indicate that the choice of allocation cost function affects which downstream metrics improve, informing future compression method design.

The Related Work section is organized by three categories (LLM Compression, Activation-Aware Methods, Rank Allocation), which is a good structural choice. However, it has three gaps that weaken the novelty positioning.

**Missing key references in Rank Allocation:** The "Rank Allocation" paragraph mentions only ROCKET and CoSpaDi. It omits several directly relevant methods:
- Swift-SVD (Qi et al., 2026): activation-aware closed-form rank allocation using output activation covariance and dynamic layer importance.
- Zero-Sum SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026): global rank allocation using whitened activation-space loss estimates with a zero-sum rule.
- IO-SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026): input-output whitened SVD with heterogeneous rank allocation based on first-order calibration loss estimates.
- ARA (Lin et al., 2025): adaptive rank allocation for SVD compression using mask-based training.

These methods are directly relevant because they also address the question of how to allocate compression budgets across layers using activation-aware or output-aware signals. Their absence makes the novelty claim appear stronger than it actually is.

**Missing accuracy-perplexity evaluation literature:** The paper discusses the accuracy-perplexity tradeoff but does not cite the evaluation literature that established perplexity as a poor proxy for task accuracy under compression (LLM-KICK, Beyond Perplexity, Khanal & Capone 2024).

Mentor Revised Version:
"Rank Allocation. Global budget allocation across layers is critical for compression quality. ROCKET (Ali et al., 2026) formulates this as a multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP). Recent work has explored activation-aware rank allocation from different angles: Swift-SVD (Qi et al., 2026) uses output activation covariance and layer importance scoring for dynamic rank assignment; Zero-Sum SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026) prunes components globally using whitened activation-space loss estimates with a zero-sum rule; and IO-SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026) combines input-output whitening with first-order calibration loss scoring. These methods share our insight that activation-aware signals improve allocation quality, but differ in their optimization frameworks. Our work specifically investigates whether the output-space error metric improves MCKP allocation in the sparse-dictionary setting of ROCKET.

Evaluation beyond Perplexity. Several studies have documented that perplexity is an incomplete proxy for compressed model quality. LLM-KICK (Jaiswal et al., 2023) shows that pruning methods degrade significantly on knowledge-intensive tasks even when perplexity is preserved. Beyond Perplexity (Xu et al., 2024) reveals divergent safety impacts across compression methods that perplexity fails to capture. Khanal & Capone (2024) introduce JS Divergence as a more comprehensive metric for behavioral shifts. Our work adds to this literature by demonstrating that the choice of allocation cost function within a single compression method can produce systematic accuracy-perplexity tradeoffs."
